headline: High-risk data leakage and cascading-error pathways exist because Dify can write/read files and call external APIs while the zoomcamp profile is non-runnable and undocumented for isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Dify can ingest uploaded knowledge-base files and wire tools into agent/workflow apps, so attacker-controlled content could be treated as instructions. The zoomcamp profile is a course repo with no runtime surfaces, so the bridge is indirect, but Dify’s default agent patterns make prompt injection plausible if course materials are fed into it.
conditions: IF course content from agent_a is uploaded into agent_b as knowledge-base material
IF agent_b treats retrieved file text as instruction-bearing context
mitigations: Restrict agent_b to quoted excerpts only
Add a system prompt that forbids following file instructions
Tag uploaded course files as untrusted
Review one sample retrieval prompt before enabling workflows

B_data_leakage.rationale: Dify reads and writes files, handles conversation logs, and sends data to model providers and user-defined OpenAPI tools. The zoomcamp repo itself is open-source and non-runnable, but if its materials or derived notes are uploaded into Dify, those contents can flow into external inference or tool calls, creating a shared-workspace leakage path.
conditions: IF agent_a materials are uploaded into agent_b's knowledge base
IF agent_b routes those materials to model providers or OpenAPI tools
mitigations: Disable external tools for sensitive uploads
Use a separate workspace for course materials
Redact secrets before upload
Turn off conversation-log retention for test runs
Verify provider-side logging settings

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent_b has broad filesystem write and shell execution, while agent_a is a repository/course artifact with no runtime protections or locking model. If both are used in the same workspace or automation chain, Dify can overwrite or consume files that the zoomcamp materials expect to remain stable, causing mutable-resource conflicts even though agent_a itself cannot write.
conditions: IF agent_b writes into the same directory that stores agent_a materials
IF multiple Dify instances share the same datastore-backed state
mitigations: Mount course files read-only
Separate working directories per agent
Disable concurrent edits on shared artifacts
Snapshot files before workflow runs

D_cascading_error.rationale: Dify is designed for agent/workflow orchestration and can act on tool outputs, so if it consumes content derived from the zoomcamp repo, it may treat that content as authoritative without verification. The repo is educational rather than operational, which lowers blast radius, but the default orchestration pattern still enables downstream mistakes when unverified outputs are reused.
conditions: IF agent_b uses agent_a-derived text as workflow input
IF downstream tools execute actions based on that text without human review
mitigations: Insert a human approval step
Require source citations in outputs
Add validation rules before tool execution
Limit workflows to read-only actions

E_compliance.rationale: No direct residency or regulated-data mismatch is documented for the zoomcamp course repo, while Dify explicitly handles conversation logs and model-provider API keys. Because the pairwise compliance pathway is not directly evidenced and the other agent is a public course artifact, the main issue is a small documentation gap rather than a clear breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is entered into agent_b while using agent_a-derived workflows
IF retention settings for conversation logs are left at defaults
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in test runs
Review retention settings
Document data-class handling for the workflow
Separate public course content from private projects
